Sandy Springs stood out because it has seen far less new apartment supply than the rest of the Atlanta metro, so demand remains strong, McCullough said in emailed comments. The development is located on a 6.9-acre site close to major highways and Metropolitan Atlanta Rapid Transit Authority transit stops. “The submarket has high household incomes, above-average occupancy, and a high cost of homeownership that supports long-term rental demand,” McCullough said. “Caldwell sits just off GA-400 and is minutes from Perimeter Center, Buckhead, and Roswell, which fits our focus on established submarkets near major employment centers.” Caldwell was designed “with a focus on wellness and functionality,” according to McCullough. It’s the first part of a multiphase development. The seven-story apartment building spans more than four acres and will include 380 parking spaces. 4600 Fairfax offers residents “seamless connectivity to Metro, retail and major employment centers in one of Northern Virginia's most vibrant neighborhoods,” per the release. The project announced $195 million in financing in May, with a senior construction loan from Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, according to the release. Residents are expected to start moving in during the first quarter of 2029. The launch of 4600 Fairfax represents Hoffman & Associates’ ongoing expansion of its residential portfolio across the Mid-Atlantic region, per the release. The site will also be prepared for construction of a separate for-sale component, with plans for a four-story penthouse south building with 29 townhome-style multifamily units plus additional apartments, according to the project website. items.title: NAMB opposes VA loan fee increases in Senate bill
items.description: The National Association of Mortgage Brokers ( NAMB ) is urging mortgage professionals to contact their senators and oppose proposed increases to fees for veterans using Department of Veterans Affairs ( VA ) home loans, arguing the changes would shift the cost of new benefits onto other veterans. The advocacy campaign, posted on NAMB's website, comes as the Senate considers S. 4744, its version of the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act (H.R. 9237), which passed the House by voice vote on Veterans Day. The Senate bill is on the calendar and is eligible for debate and a vote. NAMB supports the legislation's goal of providing additional benefits to combat-injured veterans but opposes Section 104, which would increase fees associated with VA loans. "Our biggest issue is the fact that our veterans serving our country took an oath to serve and defend. They didn't take or raise their hand to receive a bill to pay for benefits for their fallen or disabled brothers and sisters. That is not the obligation of the soldier. That's the obligation of the taxpayer and the disbursement of those tax dollars on the appropriations," NAMB President Michael Farrell said in a conversation with HousingWire . Under the Senate proposal, the funding fee for Interest Rate Reduction Refinance Loans (IRRRLs) would increase from 0.5% to 1.42%, while the VA loan assumption fee would double from 0.5% to 1%. The increases would also become permanent, eliminating a 10-year sunset provision. "For the veteran doing the IRRRL and raising that 1.42% from 0.5% on a $400,000 average loan is taking [the fee] from $2,000 to $5,680. And the the concept of, 'Well, it doesn't affect their recoupment' in regards to justifying doing the loan … it does affect and impact the cost of doing the loan," Farrell added. NAMB estimates the changes would add $4 billion in costs for veteran borrowers, or an average of $3,780 per veteran. The association also argues the higher IRRRL fee could conflict with the VA's 36-month recoupment requirement, potentially making some veterans ineligible for the refinancing program. "It seems like there's other solutions that can be looked into to raise the funding to support the benefit. … But to alienate it just to one aspect of the IRRRL, when home affordability is a huge concern and veterans are looking to step down their rate or step down their payment to better their family living expenses, now we've tripled the cost of getting that done," Farrell said. Instead, NAMB is advocating for passage of the Major Richard Star Act (H.R. 2102/S. 1032), a bipartisan, standalone measure that would allow approximately 54,000 combat-injured military retirees to receive both full retirement pay and VA disability compensation. The legislation was introduced by Rep. Gus Bilirakis (R-Fla.) in the House and by Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) in the Senate. On Veterans Day , the House voted 245-175 to discharge a resolution to consider the legislation separately and, on Nov. 12, passed the act. "We are supportive of every veteran receiving their benefit," Farrell said. "And if this is going to help 54,000 combat injured military retirees receive both their retirement pay and their disability pay, we stand to support the standalone Major Star Act. We do agree with that, but [regarding] Section 104, we have huge concerns on the feasibility of putting this bill on the backs of fellow veterans." Related More: NAMB VA Loan Veterans

items.title: Infill outlier Thomas James Homes 'landmaxxes' lots with ADUs
items.description: Where new construction is scarce and lots are tight, luxury homebuilder Thomas James Homes (TJH) has pivoted to offering accessory dwelling units (ADUs) to entice its homebuyers by adding more square footage on parcels with little room to spare. For the firm’s Pacific Northwest division, which operates in Seattle and nearby suburbs where lots are small and space is at a premium, the approach is a natural fit. While detached ADUs are the more common use case nationwide, TJH’s PNW division uses attached ADUs because they offer cost efficiencies and add functional living space to small infill lots without sacrificing as much yard. Most TJH floorplans in the region, which typically sell for $2 million to $5 million, include an attached ADU option, according to PNW division president Adam Rohde. More than half of buyers choose to include one. Founded in 2006, TJH is a high-end, scattered-lot homebuilder that operates in California, Washington and Arizona. The company specializes in building replacement homes on individual lots in established neighborhoods where new construction is limited, either on homeowner-owned lots or through spec home sales. The goal is to bring the efficiency and predictability of production building to the infill market. ADUs, which TJH began incorporating into more floor plans around 2022 or 2023, nest within that strategy by helping owners get more out of limited space, a trend the builder calls “landmaxxing.” Luxury buyers increasingly want flex space, and as Washington has passed stronger ADU laws allowing more density, TJH has used the new rules to fit more square footage on its buyers’ lots. For builders operating in dense urban and suburban markets, TJH’s playbook offers a case study in making every square foot of a lot count. “It’s our job to work with buyers to figure out how to best maximize the building value on their land,” Rohde said in an interview. “Our view of ADUs is that it's a great way to expand the amount of home you can build, which, in and of itself, is a good proposition.” Why TJH pursues attached ADUs TJH’s ADU strategy varies by division and market. While other divisions build detached ADUs, the PNW division favors attached units, which function as independent living spaces connected to the main house or built within it. Buyers use the extra space in varying ways, from a home office or gym to bonus square footage, a rental unit or a place for multigenerational living. According to Rohde, attached or integrated ADUs make more sense than detached ADUs for two main reasons. First, the company builds on smaller infill lots with limited outdoor space. A detached ADU cuts into that space more than an attached alternative. "We're typically acquiring lots that…already have limited yard space. So, to put a detached unit in, you're then eating further into that ability to create a very livable yard,” Rohde explained. Second, attached ADUs share walls with the primary residence, which reduces the amount of additional construction required. Unlike detached units, they don't require a completely separate structure, additional siding or separate utility connections. That creates efficiencies and makes them more cost-effective, with a better return on investment. “With the integrated system, you're already having some shared wall space, so you're already getting some economies of scale and efficiency that make it a lot more cost-effective than the detached-style units,” he explained. Still, that efficiency doesn’t make ADUs a simple project, and Rohde argued against the notion that they are an easy add-on, particularly detached units. “There’s this perception in the market, especially when the new regulations were hitting to allow the expansion of detached ADUs in particular, that, ‘Hey, it’s really easy. You just pick up a module, plop it in your backyard, and presto, you have additional living space,’” he said. “The reality is, it’s just frankly not that simple.” He pointed to several reasons why ADUs can be challenging to build, including fire separation and building codes, utility connections, site access and logistics, zoning and permitting timelines and the burden of ongoing maintenance costs. “What people found is that it’s not that simple. And then it became, ‘How do we integrate ADUs into a more thoughtful development process?' I think we’re really seeing a lot of traction around that [strategy],” Rohde explained. How recent legislation aids this approach Washington House Bill 1337, passed in 2023, helped make TJH’s approach possible. Under the legislation, cities statewide must allow two ADUs per lot. The legislation requires municipalities to allow ADUs with a gross floor area of at least 1,000 square feet. That legislation made it far easier for TJH to offer an attached ADU in most of its Seattle floor plans. The real density gain, according to Rohde, comes from how Seattle treats a home with an ADU as two units, which increases floor area ratio and lets TJH build more total square footage, including the integrated ADU, on the same lot within zoning limits. To comply with the law, Seattle updated its ADU rules in 2025 to treat a home with an ADU as two units, which may allow additional floor area ratio (FAR) on the lot. That allows TJH to build more total square footage when including an integrated ADU. “It allows us to build more home on a given lot,” Rohde said. “But it’s not just building square footage for the sake of building square footage. It's building thoughtful, value-add square footage.” Rohde also pointed to Washington House Bill 1096, passed in 2025, which requires qualifying cities to create an administrative process for splitting a residential lot in two. items.title: Ackman says Trump can still end GSE conservatorships, relist this term
items.description: Bill Ackman still believes Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac can be relisted on the New York Stock Exchange and exit their conservatorships before the end of President Donald Trump’s second term, even after Democrats won control of both chambers in the midterm elections. In a letter to Pershing Square Holdings shareholders signed in early November, Ackman, the company's founder and CEO, and chief investment officer Ryan Israel wrote that “a relisting and release from conservatorship can be accomplished by the President using his executive authority without any involvement of Congress ." They argue that the administration has a political incentive to act before 2029 to avoid “handing control” of the government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs) to a future administration, given the influence they have over housing policy. Ackman and Israel said the GSEs can be released “in a manner that maintains and enhances mortgage affordability while maximizing the long-term value of American taxpayers’ 79.9% ownership of the two companies.” The Department of the Treasury holds warrants to acquire 79.9% of each enterprise’s common stock. Pershing first detailed a road map in November 2025. The plan begins with a new agreement between the Treasury and the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) that addresses repayment or restructuring of Treasury’s senior preferred stock. The next step would be for the Treasury to exercise its warrants to purchase 79.9% of the GSEs' common shares. The final step would be FHFA approval for the GSEs to relist on the NYSE as privately owned operating companies. “The relisting and release of F2 will be one of the few major pieces of economic policy the President can still achieve after the midterms,” Ackman and Israel wrote. “We believe that there is no credible alternative to F2 exiting conservatorship and relisting on the NYSE as private-sector-owned operating companies.” The memo also says Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has indicated the administration will focus on the GSEs and their future ownership status in 2027 and 2028. 18 years under consevatorship Fannie and Freddie have been in conservatorship for 18 years. According to the Pershing memo, they now have more than $200 billion of shareholder equity. Over the past decade, average annual credit losses have been “only 0.05%,” and current capital levels are described as roughly 50 times that loss rate. Ackman and Israel estimate that combined capital could grow to more than $375 billion over the next five years, or more than 4% of the mortgage-backed securities guaranteed by the enterprises. On valuation, the memo says the GSEs currently trade at about 1.5 times their earnings. From Trump’s election through the end of last year, when talk of a relisting was more active, their share prices rose by about eight times. This year, by contrast, their share prices have fallen more than 60% as the administration has remained “silent” on the issue, the investors said. Pershing Square is heavily exposed to the outcome. The fund holds about 99 million shares of Fannie Mae, with a market value of roughly $422.5 million, along with roughly 95 million shares of Freddie Mac valued at about $386.9 million, according to the memo. items.title: Austin Office Campus Lands $228M Refinancing Deal
items.description: Developer Jay Paul Co. has secured $227.5M in green financing to recapitalize an 881K SF office campus in Austin. The deal marks the largest commercial property assessed clean energy, or C-PACE , transaction in Texas to date, according to Nuveen Green Capital, which closed the financing for the property. Unsplash/micheile henderson The $227.5M refinanced a construction loan on Springdale Green, a Class-A office campus at 1011 Springdale Road, Nuveen announced in a press release . C-PACE allows commercial property owners to secure long-term, low-cost financing for sustainable projects. The fixed-rate loans are often used for properties looking to make upgrades in terms of energy efficiency, water conservation and renewable energy. "The closing on Springdale Green reinforces the widespread adoption of C-PACE by institutional owners and developers," Cory Jubran, senior director of originations at Nuveen, said in an emailed statement. "C-PACE’s flexibility and lower cost of capital compared to other forms of finance are helping drive large-scale development, including notable projects like this one in Austin, across Texas, and in other MSAs." C-PACE momentum has picked up over the past couple of years, with a record $3.7B deployed in 2025, a 53% year-over-year surge, according to nonprofit PACENation. Springdale Green is a LEED Gold and Fitwel-certified property. It comprises two six-story office buildings on a 30-acre site and features a fitness center, a covered parking garage and more than 31K SF of outdoor space. Austin's office market posted strong net absorption in the third quarter, reaching 124K SF in Class-A space and 253K SF total, according to a CBRE report . That total surpassed the 50K SF posted in the second quarter as tenants took substantially more space than they vacated. Average office asking rents trended "gradually higher" throughout the quarter, with Class-A office space averaging $58.54 per SF, a 2.5% year-over-year increase, according to the report. items.title: How The Investors Upgrading Boston's Old Office Towers Are Luring New Tenants
items.description: Some of the aging office towers that define downtown Boston’s skyline are receiving face-lifts, and leasing activity this year shows they are starting to pay off. As more office buildings trade at low prices, the new owners of many of Boston’s older Class-A skyscrapers are upgrading buildings to attract tenants. These projects range from simple facade and lobby renovations to the addition of high-end amenity lounges, hospitality services and large conference rooms. In at least three cases, such renovation projects have led to a series of lease deals that have meaningfully improved a building’s occupancy. Bisnow spoke with landlords who have invested millions — and in some cases $100M — in these renovation projects about which strategies have proven successful. Courtesy of Synergy The newly renovated lobby at Synergy's 101 Arch St. "The pricing is at all-time lows, but that doesn't get you all the way there," Synergy Head of Asset Management Brian Collins said. "You do need to go one step beyond these acquisitions, and it's really a curated amenity repositioning." Synergy led the way in buying discounted Boston office buildings coming out of the pandemic, and more investors this year have followed suit. In June, Kendall Capital acquired the 11-story office building at 18 Tremont St. for $30M , roughly 29% of the $103M Jamestown paid almost seven years ago. Last month, Rockpoint Group bought back its 1.1M SF 100 Summer St. office building at a foreclosure auction for $260M , a fraction of the $806M it paid for the building in 2019. Rockpoint executives told The Boston Globe they are already looking into property upgrades for the office tower now that they were able to restructure their basis. These discounted prices are increasingly becoming available as office owners’ loans come due and lenders stop extending their maturities. This has led to more distressed deals but has also created opportunities for investors to come in at a lower basis and fund improvements that former landlords locked into pre-pandemic pricing might not have been able to make. Beacon Capital Partners Managing Director Meredith Majoch said at a Bisnow event last month that "distress is finally trading, which is a good thing." And Cambridge Savings Bank Executive Vice President Ian Brandon said a wave of loan maturities next year will create "a great deal of opportunity" for these discounted deals. One of the most notable buildings Synergy has acquired over the last five years was 101 Arch St., a 21-story office tower in Downtown Crossing , which it purchased in 2024 for $78M . The prior owner, Clarion Partners , had paid $121.7M in 2005. Synergy invested roughly $20M in the property, including building out six spec suites and shifting the tenant-only lobby from Summer Street to Arch Street. The 14-story office building was the longtime home of Boston Private Bank & Trust Co., but the bank moved out several years ago, leaving the office building 57% vacant, Collins said. The renovation project included a new lobby and exterior, updates to Synergy's office in the building, and the attraction of a new Italian restaurant concept from famous restaurant brand Coje, which already operates the Cuban restaurant Mariel in the building. 10 Post Office Square reached 89% occupancy with more than 130K SF in deals since the renovations took place last year, Collins said. items.title: Chetrit's 26 Broadway Office Tower Has Value Slashed By 68%
items.description: In the latest twist of fate for the Chetrit family, a Financial District office tower whose loan transferred to special servicing earlier this year has had its value cut dramatically. Wikimedia Commons/Ken Lund The Standard Oil Building at 26 Broadway The Standard Oil Building at 26 Broadway received a new appraisal of $147M, according to Morningstar Credit . That’s down 68% from the $465M value that was reported when it was last appraised in 2021. The owners took out a new $290M mortgage the following year, provided by Starwood Mortgage Capital and the Bank of Montreal and backed by the 840K SF office tower. But the debt has been troubled since earlier this year, when it moved to special servicing after the borrower said it wouldn’t be able to keep making payments. That came as the building was facing problems. Its cash flow was 30% down from the levels at which the debt was underwritten, according to Morningstar, and occupancy had fallen from 82% at the time its loan was originated to 75% at the end of March 2026. Morningstar lists Meyer and Jacob Chetrit as the loan’s sponsors, while Jacob signed for the mortgage in public records in 2022. Meyer Chetrit didn't respond to a request for comment. After Jacob Chetrit died in January 2025 , the Chetrit Group entered a chapter of turmoil as questions surfaced about how the family firm’s former real estate empire could fend off mounting troubles. The Chetrit Group defaulted on a $481M loan tied to a Chetrit portfolio in 2022. In 2025, Wells Fargo sued JPMorgan Chase , alleging that the portfolio’s net operating income had been overinflated and naming Meyer Chetrit as a defendant. A judge allowed the case to proceed this spring. The Chetrits were struck with tenant harassment claims at a Chelsea apartment building and sued by the city for violations at the Hotel Carter in 2025. Meyer and Joseph Chetrit were also subpoenaed earlier in the year , revealing details about the Chetrit Group’s finances. Meyer Chetrit testified in March that the organization was out of funds and that its portfolio value had dropped from around $964M at the end of 2022 to negative $80M. items.title: Aging Parents and Empty Nests Force Homeowners To Rethink Layouts Years Before the Move
items.description: Most homeowners know their homes may need updates to accommodate their changing needs as they age. Some, however, are thinking even further ahead. Instead of waiting until those changes are necessary, they’re investing in renovations years in advance to prepare for aging parents who might eventually move in after their children leave the nest. Angi’s 2026 State of Home Spending Pulse study found that 66% of homeowners plan to make a major home investment within the next five years. And the 2027 Home Trends To Watch report predicts that 2027 will be the year they take a proactive approach and focus on creating a home that grows with them. If you own your home, experts agree that you should anticipate how your needs could change in the next five to 10 years and use that information to guide your long-term home improvement goals today. By doing so, you can make the most out of your renovation budget, avoid costly last-minute adjustments, and ensure your home comfortably adapts to the different stages of life. What's driving this trend? Matt Plaskoff, CEO and founder of One Week Bath in Los Angeles , is seeing this proactive, multigenerational "future-proofing” trend among his clients. “It comes down to people having heard stories of it going the other way. Mom falls or receives a diagnosis, and suddenly the family is trying to put in a walk-in shower and grab bars on short notice while suddenly incurring more costs with doctors and insurance,” says Plaskoff. Multigenerational living is also at an all-time high, and the recent National Association of Realtors® Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers report reflects this shift. It found that 17% of homes purchased last year were intended for multigenerational households. And when adult kids leave, there’s suddenly more space that makes it easier to create a home that works well for both aging in place and aging parents. We can’t forget the housing affordability crisis forcing families to rethink the homes they already own. “The house may no longer fit the household, but buying a better-fitting home can mean a higher price, a higher mortgage rate, and higher monthly expenses,” says Jon Brooks , co-founder of Momentum Realty in Jacksonville, FL . Plus, it's more cost-effective to future-proof your home when you plan properly and actually have the funds to support your projects. “The worst time to remodel is when you don’t have the budget for it. You make decisions that should take time and careful planning under pressure and may just accept whatever contractor can show up ASAP, even if it means you have to pay more,” says Plaskoff. There is also a practical side. If you're already opening up walls for a bath remodel, for example, adding blocking for future grab bars, widening a doorway, or adding a curbless shower will be faster and cheaper than if you were to come back later and redo finished work. Loading... If you're thinking about starting a new remodeling project, think ahead to your needs. Realtor.com/Getty Images Balancing safety, privacy, and resale Experts agree that a strong universal design features a functional yet beautiful bathroom with a wider doorway, good lighting, lever handles for knobs, a walk-in shower, and slip-resistant flooring. “If done right, it feels more like a spa than a hospital, and that’s what matters most to those who are using it every day,” Plaskoff explains. A home that supports privacy and independence is just as important. “An example can be a primary suite on the ground floor with its own bathroom, or a room with a separate entrance. Parents want to keep their routines and privacy, without having to sacrifice accessibility,” says Plaskoff. You might also consider adding a second structure to your backyard like an accessory dwelling unit or tiny home. “For families with the space, an ADU is one of the best solutions we see. It gives an aging parent true independence, with their own kitchen, bath, and front door, while keeping them close enough for daily connection and support,” explains Michelle Squire , designer and principal at Studio SQUARE in San Francisco . If long-term resale is important to you, be sure to consider what buyers value in your neighborhood. This way you can determine where to make permanent changes and where to keep things flexible. “If you’re overimproving for the area, just understand you may have a harder time recouping that money if you choose to sell,” says Christina Rordam , real estate agent at Florida Realty Investments in Orlando, FL . At the end of the day, prioritize flexibility, try not to over improve for the neighborhood you’re in, and most importantly, consider what works best for you and your family.

items.title: Inside the Properties James Bond Has Made Famous as Robert Pattinson Gears Up to Play 007
items.description: It’s official: Robert Pattinson is stepping into the role of James Bond . The news comes after years of speculation surrounding who might succeed Daniel Craig —who was the sixth actor to bring 007 to life, and portrayed the British spy in five films, ending with 2021’s “No Time To Die.” The official James Bond X account shared a first look of Pattinson donning the infamous tux for the role, captioned “Identity Confirmed.” “James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement . “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement.” Director Denis Villeneuve alluded to the search for the next Bond in the statement. Loading... Robert Pattinson has been announced as the next James Bond. He's the seventh actor to bring Agent 007 to life. Photo by Dia Dipasupil/Getty Images “I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey,” the “Dune” director said. “We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007.” Dozens of potential candidates have been floated as possibilities since Craig’s reign came to an end, including Idris Elba , Jacob Elordi , Callum Turner , and John Hardy . Bond first walked onto the silver screen in 1962, when Sean Connery brought the iconic book character to life in the first film, “Dr. No.” There have been a whopping 25 Bond films so far, with Pattinson suiting up for the 26th. After seven films, Connery ended his run in 1983 with “Never Say Never.” In 1969, George Lazenby became the only actor to star in a single film in the franchise, with “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service.” Roger Moore held the role from 1973 to 1985, also impressively holding the gig for seven titles. Next up was Timothy Dalton , who starred in two films between 1987 and 1989. Pierce Brosnan reinvigorated the franchise when he became Bond in 1995, holding the job until 2002. In 2006, Craig ushered in a new era, tackling 007 with a more rough-and-tumble edge. Perhaps even more impressive than the scale of actors who have taken their martinis shaken, not stirred, is the sheer number of filming locations the franchise has made its mark on for over 60 years. Hunting Bond, a fan site that tracks the locations, has identified nearly 600 filming spots across the world. While the James Bond universe is certainly action-packed, it’s also quite aspirational, and has often provided viewers with rich backgrounds and fascinating properties that became characters in their own right. It would be nearly impossible to rank all of the lavish homes Bond has stepped foot in over the years, but there are definitely a handful that stand out in memory. The home was built for interior designer Arthur Elrod. Realtor.com Loading... In the film, Sean Connery's Bond pushes an enemy into the home's half-moon pool. Bob Penn/Sygma/Sygma via Getty Images Even without a connection to one of the Bond films with the strongest pop culture staying power—”Diamonds Are Forever,” of course— the Elrod House in Palm Springs, CA , is an incredible dwelling. Perched on a hillside overlooking Coachella Valley, the 8,900-square-foot home was designed by modernist architect John Lautner for interior designer Arthur Elrod . The fascinating structure has a concrete dome-shaped roof, a circular living room, and a half-moon swimming pool that Connery’s Bond threw an enemy into during a heated fight scene. Villa Sylva Loading... A Greek property overlooking the Ionian Sea, called Villa Sylva, served as a backdrop in "For Your Eyes Only." Google Earth Loading... In the Roger Moore-led film, the estate is assumed to be in Madrid. Oscar Abolafia/TPLP/Getty Images Villa Sylva is a picturesque Greek estate that’s appeared in a handful of movies, including Moore’s “For Your Eyes Only”—although in the film, it assumed the role of the Madrid home of hitman Hector Gonzales. The 12-bedroom luxury villa boasts unobstructed views of the Ionian Sea and is perched on an idyllic 10-acre property. Today, it can be rented as a wedding venue or a vacation home sleeping up to 18 people. Luton Hoo Estate Loading... Luton Hoo, a distinguished estate an hour's drive from London, has appeared in dozens of projects, including two Bond films. Tony Evans/Getty Images Loading... The property was a filming location in Pierce Brosnan's 1999 film, "The World Is Not Enough," as well as Sean Connery's 1983 flick, "Never Say Never Again." Keith Hamshere/Getty Images Given Bond’s important role at the UK-based M16, it only makes sense that at least some of the locations had to be local. The sprawling Luton Hoo Estate was a location in Brosnan’s 1999 film, “The World Is Not Enough” and Connery’s 1983 return for “Never Say Never Again.” It’s also been featured in dozens of other projects, including “Downton Abbey.” Built in 1903, the property is about an hour’s drive from London—a journey that would probably be cut in half when Bond is behind the wheel. The historic English country estate spans more than 1,000 acres and has a handful of structures—most notably, a five-star hotel and an exquisite mansion. The Ocean Club Loading... "Casino Royale" took viewers to the picturesque Bahamas. Google Earth Loading... Daniel Craig's Bond stays at a villa in the breathtaking Ocean Club and takes a dip in the gorgeous water. items.title: Nantucket Brokerage Must Pay $1.3 Million to Buyers Who Couldn’t Expand Their Home as Desired
items.description: A Massachusetts judge and jury have ordered a Nantucket real estate firm to pay nearly $1.3 million to a couple after finding that one of its agents misrepresented whether a home could be expanded to fit their family of eight. The years-long legal battle centered on a 2-bedroom, 1,200 square-foot property purchased by Dr. Mary Murray and Jeff Ment. Murray, an obstetrician, and Ment, a lawyer, live in Westport, CT , but spend summers with their six children in Nantucket, MA. Their kids “all love to be there. Every single one of them loves to be on the island, and we love to be with them,” Murray tells Realtor.com® . Their real estate agent, Melanie Gowen , helped them find rentals in previous years, and in 2020 she represented them in their purchase of 151 P olpis Rd . for $1.41 million. Murray says the home wasn’t ideal, but in the ultra-competitive Nantucket market, where the median listing price is $5.995 million, they felt lucky to buy anything at all. And Murray says the family was reassured after, Gowen, an agent with William Raveis Nantucket, told the couple they’d have no problem building an addition to accommodate their six children. “She said, ‘Listen, I know it’s the smallest house. But it’s a great buy. The best part about this is it’s an undersized house on an oversized piece of property that you can double,’” Murray says. According to the couple, Gowen said she went to the island’s building department and confirmed expansion was possible. She’d even sketched out the addition and sent a video of the planned build, Murray said. In Nantucket, specific rules govern how many bedrooms a home can be zoned for. But Ment said Gowen openly discussed how a homeowner could get around those rules by calling an addition a den or a living room, then adding a bed. “In writing, she had told us, ‘I know you can't call anything a bedroom, but you can do what's always done on Nantucket and call it some other room and use it as a bedroom,” Ment said. In early 2021, Murray and Ment began planning the addition and contacted the town about a septic upgrade and expansion and learned that “absolutely not another inch or square foot can be added to the property,” Murray said. “That's when everything started to crystallize that it wasn't quite as advertised,” Ment added. Loading... The median listing price for homes on exclusive Nantucket Island is $5.995 million. Google Earth Without an addition, the home was too small for their family and essentially useless to the couple. Ment and Murray confronted Gowen. “She tells us we're incorrect, that of course it can be doubled,” Ment says. “We say we don't think we're incorrect, but, you know, go ahead and do what you can do.” She then called back with her colleague, Kenny Hilbig , on the line. Hilbig told the couple, “Turns out it can't be expanded due to a deed restriction. And we're gonna work with you to figure this out,” Ment recalls. Hilbig initially suggested that they might be able to “trade” their property for another home. “He knew of some other properties that were coming on the market," Ment says. "He thought we could basically trade a house somehow.” But that idea didn't come to fruition. Hilbig then suggested that the brokerage William Raveis Nantucket might give the couple a bridge loan to purchase a third home. The company nixed that option as well. Murray and Ment claim Hilbig then told them the only way they could recoup anything from the brokerage directly was to sue. So in June 2021, Murray and Ment filed a lawsuit in Norfolk Superior Court. The couple sued Gowen and William Raveis for misrepresentation; negligence; breach of contract; breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing; breach of fiduciary duty; and violation of the Massachusetts Consumer Protection Act, otherwise known as 93A, for willfully and knowingly making unverified misrepresentations in trade/commerce and failing to make a reasonable settlement offer after receiving a formal demand letter. The lawsuit alleged that “Since Dr. Murray and Mr. Ment had been working with Ms. Gowen for so long, they trusted her, her opinions, recommendations, referrals, and relied on her island knowledge. Ms. Gowen had represented that she possessed experience both building and designing homes on the Island of Nantucket. Ms. Gowen held herself out as not only a real estate agent but as an interior designer and property developer.” In January, a jury awarded Murray and Ment $1.28 million in damages. Loading... Jeffrey Ment and Mary Murray said they purchased the 2-bedroom home on Polpis Rd. because they wanted to have a summer base for their family. items.title: When mortgage reviewers disagree with AI: A practical adjudication protocol
items.description: An AI system flags a problem in a mortgage file. The reviewer looks at the documents and disagrees. During an evaluation, this can become a discussion about whether the technology works. In production, it becomes a decision someone has to make while the file is waiting. The system may have identified a genuine issue. The reviewer may have information the system did not receive. Both may be looking at the same evidence and interpreting a requirement differently. Putting a person in the process does not settle any of this. The team still needs a reliable way to establish what is correct. In my recent HousingWire article , I argued that lenders should measure how much human attention a loan consumes. Disagreements between AI and reviewers deserve particular attention because resolving them can take far more effort than identifying the original issue. I believe lenders should agree on how to resolve these cases before an evaluation begins. Otherwise, the evaluation can end with a long list of overrides and very little clarity about what the results mean. Preserve what the system actually found The original finding should remain available after a reviewer challenges it. That record should include the document and page involved, the data used, the requirement being tested and the relevant system or rule version. The reviewer’s response should sit alongside it, with the evidence supporting the disagreement. Consider an illustrative example in which a system flags a missing signature, but the reviewer says it is present on a later version of the document. Before deciding whether the finding was wrong, the team needs to establish which version the system reviewed and when the later version became available. If the document arrived after the review, the finding may have been correct when it was raised. If the document was already available but the system failed to select it, there is a different problem to fix. A final status of “cleared” would hide that distinction. Preserving the original evidence gives the team something concrete to investigate and prevents a later reviewer from having to reconstruct the entire discussion. Separate the fact from the interpretation A finding often contains more than one conclusion. In the signature example, one question is whether a signature appears in the relevant location. Another is whether that signature is required for the document, transaction and stage of the process being reviewed. The first is an observation, while the second depends on the applicable requirement. A system could get the observation right and apply the wrong requirement. A reviewer could correctly question the requirement but overlook that the document being reviewed is incomplete. These should be recorded as separate issues. I would ask the team to identify exactly where the disagreement sits: document selection, extracted information, applicable requirement or judgment about the issue’s significance. That distinction helps the team choose the corrective action. Improving document recognition will not resolve an unclear policy, and more reviewer training will not repair a system that consistently selects an outdated document. It also keeps the discussion focused on evidence rather than on whether the reviewer or the technology should be trusted more. Give someone clear authority to resolve it Every disputed finding needs an owner who can make the relevant decision, with that authority established before the disagreement occurs. A straightforward document-selection error may be resolved within the review team. A question about how a requirement applies may need a designated policy owner, while a recurring technical error should reach the team responsible for the system. For material cases, I would use a second qualified reviewer rather than leaving the original reviewer to be the sole judge of their own decision. The same principle applies to the technology provider. A provider can explain its output, but should not be the only party deciding whether that output meets the lender’s requirements. The resolution should state what was decided, the evidence relied upon and who approved it. “Reviewer disagreed” tells the next person very little. The process should also be proportionate. An obvious extraction error should not require a committee. A disputed issue that could affect a consequential decision deserves more scrutiny. Allow the answer to remain unresolved Sometimes the available evidence will not support a decision because a document is unreadable, a required page is missing or the relevant requirement needs clarification. Forcing the case into “AI correct” or “reviewer correct” in those circumstances creates certainty the team has not earned. The case should remain unresolved, with the missing evidence or clarification identified and the next action assigned. That status should have an owner and a review date. It should also have a defined consequence for the workflow, based on the nature of the issue and the lender’s existing controls. An unresolved disagreement should not silently disappear because the file has moved to another team. During an evaluation, unresolved cases should remain visible in the results. They should not be counted as successes or quietly removed from the reported sample. This matters when comparing systems. A strong accuracy figure is difficult to interpret if the hardest cases have been excluded because no one could establish the correct answer. Measure what it took to reach the answer The resolution itself is only part of the result. Lenders should also examine how much time the reviewer spent finding the evidence, whether another person had to repeat the review and whether the file was reopened. They should track whether the same issue returned on the next loan. These questions reveal whether the technology is making the work easier. items.title: The next housing crisis could be a cyberattack, not a rate shock
items.description: For decades, the mortgage industry has understood risk through interest rates, credit performance, liquidity and market volatility. We have sophisticated models to anticipate financial disruptions and regulatory frameworks designed to manage them. Often overlooked is the security and resilience of the digital infrastructure that makes American homeownership possible. Every day, servicing platforms move escrow payments, safeguard homeowners’ data and support families through hardship. An attack on these systems is not just an IT problem. It represents a significant financial risk to millions of American families. The next disruption to the housing market may not begin with a change in interest rates. It could start with a compromised identity, an exploited vulnerability or an attack on a critical technology provider. Protecting these systems starts with a mindset shift. Servicers should approach their platforms with a Zero Trust philosophy, trusting nothing by default and building and running every system under the assumption that it can be compromised. Security must be engineered in, not bolted on One of the most persistent mistakes in enterprise technology is treating cybersecurity as something that happens after software is built, a gap that cybercriminals are quick to exploit. Weak architecture, excessive privileges, insecure integrations and misconfigured infrastructure get baked into a system, and fixing them after deployment costs far more than preventing them in design. Cybersecurity must be integrated into the work of every team from day one as they build new products that make loan servicing more efficient. Security should not be the department that tells engineering why something cannot go to production. It should be part of the engineering process that ensures it can go to production safely. From perimeter security to zero trust For too long, enterprise cybersecurity has assumed that if you build a strong perimeter, you can trust what’s inside it. That approach is incompatible with today’s interconnected financial ecosystem, which runs on cloud infrastructure, third-party integrations, distributed workforces and constantly shifting data flows. Zero trust is not a marketing slogan; it is an engineering philosophy that must be built in from day one and extend across the enterprise technology system. This means eliminating implicit trust and continuously evaluating access. A good lock on the front door doesn’t make a home secure if everything inside is open to anyone who gets past it. Zero trust starts with the assumption that someone eventually will get through, so every room, and the safe inside it, has its own lock. For servicers , that means a single stolen password or compromised vendor connection can’t open every borrower file and escrow account. In mortgage technology, secure by design and default must become baseline expectations rather than competitive differentiators. A proactive operational approach By adopting the Zero Trust mindset, servicers should continuously test their defenses and identify potential threats. Traditional cybersecurity programs have invested heavily in vulnerability scanning, security assessments, compliance reporting and incident response. To do this, we must move from passive defense to proactive cyber operations. Threat intelligence should be more than vulnerability scans or security assessments in a weekly report. It should directly inform how security teams hunt for threats, test defenses, prioritize engineering work and anticipate adversary behavior. Vulnerability mitigation in the modern mortgage environment Cybersecurity programs often measure success by vulnerabilities found, tickets opened and assessments completed, but those track activity, not security. Finding a vulnerability does not make an organization safer. Mitigating it does. To effectively stand up to the growing danger of cybersecurity threats, leaders should focus on shortening the time between identifying a weakness and eliminating or containing the risk. That starts with preventing vulnerabilities from entering production and continues through automated detection, intelligent prioritization, remediation and validation throughout the life of a system. The goal is not to produce a more comprehensive inventory of problems. It is to systematically reduce the opportunities available to attackers. That is the difference between vulnerability management and vulnerability mitigation. Agentic AI can change the speed of defense Artificial intelligence (AI) is already changing the threat landscape, and defenders cannot expect to prevail by relying solely on human-speed defense. Agentic AI offers a solution. Security agents can continuously correlate threat intelligence with enterprise assets, identify exploitable attack paths, orchestrate approved mitigations, confirm they were successful and escalate complex decisions to human operators. In software development, AI-enabled agents can identify insecure code, validate dependencies, evaluate infrastructure configurations, generate security tests and propose remediations before vulnerabilities reach production, helping security expertise scale across development teams. That capability must operate within carefully engineered boundaries: Zero trust identities, least-privilege access, auditable actions, appropriate testing and human oversight for consequential changes. AI-generated code and directed actions must be tested for security risk, and any AI built into products needs its access to data and systems governed from the start. Cyber resilience is a responsibility to homeowners None of this matters if we lose sight of whom we are protecting. Behind every mortgage account is a person or family making one of the most significant financial commitments of their lives. items.title: Homebuilder confidence sinks to a 14-year low as buyers hibernate
items.description: Homebuilder confidence fell in November to its lowest point since the latter days of the Global Financial Crisis, as elevated mortgage rates , persistent inflation and buyer hesitancy continue to weigh on demand. The National Association of Home Builders (NAHB)/ Wells Fargo Housing Market Index (HMI) fell four points to 25 in November, representing the weakest homebuilder confidence reading since April 2012. Builders have relied ever more heavily on discounts and mortgage buydown tactics to move inventory, with NAHB reporting that 46% of builders cut prices during the month, the highest share since the onset of the Covid-19 pandemic. Typical discounts ran flat at 6% for the eighth straight month, and 68% of builders used sales incentives, another post-Covid high. It was the 20th consecutive month that at least 60% of builders had featured margin-eroding price-cut promotions. Further, in November, all three of the key HMI components sank. The index of current sales conditions declined six points to 28, while the measure of sales expectations over the next six months slipped two points to 30, signaling a prolonged pessimistic outlook. Meanwhile, the gauge of prospective buyer traffic dropped two points to 16, the lowest level in 15 years outside of the early months of the pandemic in 2020. “Builders are confronting multiple challenges in today’s economy,” NAHB Chairman Bill Owens, a home builder and remodeler from Worthington, Ohio, said in a statement. “Stepped-up immigration enforcement is keeping legal workers off job sites, deepening labor shortages and driving up costs. Higher fuel prices are prompting subcontractors to raise their rates sharply, and with fewer buyers in the market, more builders are scaling back construction.” NAHB Chief Economist Robert Dietz said in a statement that a combination of policy and macroeconomic pressures is straining both supply and demand. “The housing market faces a range of supply-side challenges, including building material costs pushed higher by tariffs, an ongoing shortage of construction workers and excessive regulations that undermine housing affordability,” Dietz said. “Mortgage rates above 7%, softer consumer confidence and an uncertain economic outlook are holding buyers back.” Public homebuilders echoed that picture on recent earnings calls, citing hesitant buyers, heavier discounting and thinner margins. Affordability constraints keep buyers on the sidelines Century Communities Executive Chairman Dale Francescon , during an earnings call on October 28, noted that high mortgage rates , continued inflation and macroeconomic uncertainty weighed heavily on consumer confidence, particularly among first-time buyers. “As we moved through the quarter, our buyers became more cautious, did not feel an urgency to transact and felt more comfortable moving to the sidelines,” Francescon said during the call. It's not that buyers have abandoned the market. Rather, they are waiting out volatility and elongating decision-making timelines. At the same time, the number of households that can qualify for a mortgage at today's borrowing costs and sales prices continues to shrink. LGI Homes chairman and CEO Eric Lipar noted the increasingly challenging market conditions during an earnings call on November 3. “As expected, the market became more challenging as the quarter progressed,” Lipar said. “Affordability remained the defining story of the quarter.” The homebuilder, which primarily serves rate- and payment-sensitive entry-level buyers, reported a cancellation rate of 53.8%, compared with 33.6% a year earlier and 26.2% two years ago. While this trend was an outlier among most of its public homebuilding peers, it underscores how strained entry-level buyers are right now. During PulteGroup ’s earnings call on October 22, the builder’s president and CEO Ryan Marshall agreed that market conditions have become more challenging in recent months, leading many buyers to put their homebuying process on the back burner. “What changed in the quarter…is that the big move higher in interest rates, along with inflation, global tensions, and waning confidence, reached the point where more consumers simply put their search on pause,” he said during the call. Traffic to PulteGroup communities fell 14% year over year and 11% sequentially in the third quarter, with first-time buyers making up most of the missing traffic. Marshall also noted that, with 30-year mortgage rates still sitting at around 7.5% , move-up buyers are increasingly having a difficult time selling their current home, further dragging on homebuying demand. “One of the biggest impediments that we're seeing right now is that our move-up and active-adult buyers need to sell their existing home, and that is tough,” Marshall noted. With homeownership increasingly out of reach for the average working American, renting has become the more affordable option. Zillow research found that renting a home costs more than $1,000 less per month than buying one, a gap that draws many would-be buyers away from for-sale homebuilders and toward the rental market. Incentives continue to pressure margins For many homebuilders, winning over cautious buyers now means resorting to more and more incentives, in effect paying for sales. Concessions are climbing, and total sales prices are coming down with them. The median new-home sales price in September was about $400,000 , down nearly 4.0% from a year ago. items.title: Dark Matter, ServiceLink add automated closing to Empower
items.description: Dark Matter Technologies and ServiceLink have partnered to bring automated title, valuation and closing services to lenders using Dark Matter ’s Empower loan origination system. The partnership integrates ServiceLink ’s Accelerated Close platform, powered by its NowIntelligence technology, into Empower. The service automates title and valuation orders, as well as closing orders, and allows lenders or borrowers to schedule appraisals and closings. Using loan data, Accelerated Close automatically determines whether a loan qualifies for an expedited workflow. NowIntelligence evaluates eligibility using real-time market intelligence, including public and proprietary data, vendor information and market analytics. For eligible loans, Empower automatically places title and valuation orders with ServiceLink through Exchange, Dark Matter’s partner marketplace. Once a loan reaches clear-to-close status, closing orders are also placed automatically through Empower. The companies said the integration reduces manual work for lender operations teams and can shorten the time between underwriting approval and a scheduled closing. Borrower expectations are also driving demand for faster and more flexible closing processes. According to ServiceLink’s 2026 State of Homebuying Report, 82% of borrowers believe a refinance should take less than a month to close, while 87% said the ability to schedule their own appraisal or closing would influence their choice of lender. “Borrowers judge their lender by how fast and frictionless the process feels, and knowing when their appraisal and closing will happen matters a great deal,” said Vikas Rao , CEO of Dark Matter Technologies. “Accelerated Close takes routine ordering off lenders’ plates and, if desired, puts scheduling in borrowers’ hands, so loans close faster and borrowers feel in control of one of the biggest financial decisions of their lives.” ServiceLink CEO Chris Azur said the integration is intended to help lenders shorten cycle times, improve pull-through rates and provide borrowers with a more streamlined experience. For lenders, shorter cycle times could also reduce costs associated with extended rate locks. Orders placed through ServiceLink will continue to use the existing Exchange workflow for order status updates, documents and messaging. Lenders can enable Accelerated Close through their Dark Matter or ServiceLink account managers, through self-service configuration or as part of a new Empower implementation, the companies' release stated. items.title: How reverse mortgage LOs can help borrowers to self-service
items.description: Reverse mortgage servicers are investing in portals, mobile applications and smarter phone systems so borrowers can manage their loans without contacting a human customer service representative. Servicing executives say that loan officers can play a key role in whether these tools actually work. Gail Balettie , senior vice president of client satisfaction at Celink , and Ryan McIntire , director of reverse mortgage servicing controls at Onity Mortgage , outlined their companies' self-service offerings during a panel discussion moderated by Chris Downey of CrossCountry Mortgage at last week's National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA) Annual Meeting & Expo . "In today's world, where we are conditioned to some extent to be able to go online, get immediate satisfaction, to do things without talking to somebody, the more we can do that, the better we can reach our customers," McIntire said. Mobile apps and online portals Balettie announced at NRMLA Annual that her company's mobile app, ReverseLink, will be launching "in the next few weeks." Its design is similar to Celink's website and borrowers will receive an invitation to download it. The company is the largest independent subservicer of reverse mortgages and has an estimated market share of about 75% across federally insured Home Equity Conversion Mortgages (HECMs) and proprietary loans. McIntire told the audience that Onity 's servicing app is already available on iPhone and Android devices and mirrors its borrower portal. He stressed the importance of providing familiar technology to senior homeowners so "they don't feel like they're having to learn something all over again." Celink's soon-to-be-released app will allow clients to accomplish multiple tasks, Balettie said. They'll be able to request payoff quotes, make voluntary payments , upload forms and download up to two years of statements. The app automatically generates confirmation that an uploaded form has been received, cutting down the number of calls needed for this purpose. "They can request a line-of-credit draw, and if they do so, they're going to get their funds a day or two faster than the typical five-day turn time, because it comes in an automated fashion," she added. ReverseLink also has a number of FAQs and educational videos, covering subjects like how to manage the account online, what happens to the reverse mortgage when the borrower dies, how to shop for insurance coverage and how to file a claim, and how to find help with small home repairs . Onity's portal ties into the company's system of record, McIntire said. It shows three months of transactions and includes an introduction package that's tailored to the structure of the loan — for example, any funds set aside for required repairs. Onity is also in the process of building fully digital draw request forms. Today, borrowers have to download and complete these forms before returning it via email or fax, but the goal is to process e-signed draw requests within a few business days, McIntire said. "Obviously, information that's available to the borrower via this site is very sensitive. We obviously, as servicers, have to be very cognizant and mindful of fraud . So it does have multifactor authentication that just helps provide that additional sense of security," he added. Closing checklist for loan officers Borrowers commonly contact their loan officer, rather than their servicer, when they have questions about their loan. Balettie said that LOs can take an "ABCD" role to approach to providing assistance in this area. Authorized third parties Borrower portal Contact information Direct deposit Making sure a servicer has the correct contact information for a borrower may seem obvious, but it doesn't happen with perfect uniformity. "We get about 70% of our loans that board with an email address. I want to see that be 100%," Balettie said. "I don't know very many people who don't have an email address in this day and age." Balettie sought to distinguish between the alternate contact on the loan application and an authorized third party. The latter may discuss the account but cannot change contact information or request a draw or payoff. Conversely, servicers use the alternate contact only when they cannot reach the borrower, she said. In response to an audience question, Balettie said that loan officers are welcome to call a servicer on their client's behalf, but to receive a relevant response, they must be listed as the authorized third party. This is especially important for brokers, who lose access to information once a loan is sold. "We have privacy laws we have to follow," she added. A power of attorney can act for a living borrower, but legal authority ends at death, the panelists noted. Downey urged originators to execute the authorized party form at closing and warned that without it, payoffs for a borrower "can be a nightmare." Having this information on file removes the need to hire an attorney to search for heirs after the borrower dies. Balettie said originators should collect a canceled check and the direct deposit form at closing. Borrowers without a check can provide a redacted bank statement or bank letter with their account and routing numbers. Due to security concerns, servicers don't allow bank details to be added online, but they'll accept faxed or emailed documents, and closing is the best time to gather them. items.title: HSBC Sells $300M Of Data Center Debt Tied To Stargate Project At Big Discount
items.description: Financial giant HSBC has sold $300M in data center construction debt at less than 90 cents on the dollar, the latest sign of lender wariness of the growing risks facing large-scale data center development. Wikimedia Commons/Barry Caruth The debt is part of an $18B financing package assembled by 20 banks for Project Jupiter, a massive data center development in Doña Ana County, New Mexico, Bloomberg reports . The construction financing closed last year after being marketed to lenders under the code name Project Miner amid a boom in debt financing for hyperscalers ’ artificial intelligence campuses. But Project Jupiter has since run into problems. The 1,400-acre campus is being developed by Blue Owl-backed Stack Infrastructure for OpenAI , Oracle and SoftBank 's Stargate initiative and could eventually reach 2.45 gigawatts. The project has faced concerns about potential delays due to community opposition and regulatory hurdles involving air and pipeline permits. In September, Oracle sent the developers a force majeure notice that would allow it to defer payments if the project is delayed or derailed. HSBC reportedly unloaded the $300M chunk of its debt tied to the project immediately after the force majeure notice, according to Bloomberg. HSBC isn't the only lender that has tried to reduce its exposure to Project Jupiter. Dutch bank ING is also reportedly seeking buyers for $25M of debt backing the development, along with nearly a dozen other data center loans. The debt sales are just the latest sign of growing volatility across data center credit markets. Lenders are showing concerns about escalating risks surrounding data center development — from community opposition and restrictive regulations to uncertainty about the future of AI cloud providers and alarm at the pace of hyperscale infrastructure spending. Jensen Huang ’s sudden resignation from Nvidia has only added to the unease surrounding the sector. Lender anxiety has been most apparent in the structured debt markets. In recent weeks, yields on some bonds tied to data center projects have climbed into the double digits, while even debt issued by major hyperscalers has traded at higher spreads than the investment-grade standard. At the same time, credit default swaps on data center debt have hit an all-time high. Analysts also say the lenders are concerned about concentration risk . The scale of capital required for the AI data center boom is unprecedented, and there is only so much capital that any lender is comfortable having tied up in just a handful of companies all pursuing broadly similar strategies. items.title: New City Guidance Could Kill Rent Overcharge Lawsuits
items.description: Some of New York City’s biggest apartment owners notched a win this week after the city issued new guidance for calculating rent increases in stabilized apartments. Google Maps 300 Ashland Place, a property owned by Two Trees where attorneys claimed the landlord overcharged tenants of rent-stabilized units Landlords that operate buildings with rent-stabilized units, including buildings with 421-a tax subsidies, have been facing lawsuits claiming that they overcharged tenants. Defendants include Two Trees , former Gov. Eliot Spitzer’s firm and Rockrose — all of which have been named in a slew of suits filed since August. But this week, the Division of Housing and Community Renewal updated its fact sheet for those landlords, effectively undermining the argument made by tenants and their lawyers. “The updated fact sheet basically kicks the legs out from the claims that have been filed,” said YuhTyng Patka , co-chair of the NYC real estate tax and zoning incentives practice at Adler & Stachenfeld. In the suits, landlords have faced claims that they collected more rent than they were legally entitled to. The claims center on the math behind rent increases for rent-stabilized units. Prior to the 2019 Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act, landlords followed DHCR guidelines stating that increases could be calculated off the preferential rent, a term used to describe the full rent of an apartment without concessions. HSTPA removed the distinction between preferential rents and rent concessions, The Real Deal reported . But DHCR didn’t issue guidance directing landlords to make their calculations any differently, attorneys told Bisnow . Now, suits allege that rent increases for stabilized units should instead have been calculated based on the net effective rent, meaning the total rent collected when discounts are taken into account. For example, if an apartment is rented at $5K a month but a tenant is given two months of free rent, that brings the net effective rent to $4K a month, said Jeffrey Goldman, founding and co-managing partner of Belkin Burden Goldman, the firm that has been defending landlords in some of these suits. The argument that tenant attorneys are making is that the increase — limited to specific percentages by the Rent Guidelines Board — should be based on the $4K rather than the $5K in that case, he said. Many landlords handed out concessions just like this to tenants in recent years, Goldman said, adding that it is still a frequent occurrence when a building is in its initial lease-up period if the building’s amenities aren’t available yet and during the slower leasing period in the winter months. “That practice was longstanding. It was not uncommon,” Patka said. “It was known by [the NYC Department of Housing Preservation and Development] and DHCR, who did not say or do anything to discourage the practice.” But an April ruling from New York County Supreme Court Judge Arlene Bluth, on a case known as Grey v. LIC Development Owner, changed the calculation for concessions, The Real Deal previously reported . That decision set off a wave of lawsuits aimed at landlords including Fetner Properties , Gotham Organization , Douglaston Development and The Durst Organization , according to Adler & Stachenfeld data shared with Bisnow . One firm alone, Newman Ferrera, filed 21 such suits between August and early November, according to Adler & Stachenfeld. However, the 2019 HSTPA law didn’t mention concessions, Adler & Stachenfeld NYC real estate tax and zoning incentives associate Zachary Nathanson said. With DHCR’s publication of an updated fact sheet regarding calculating rent increases, Bluth’s ruling will make it much harder for many of those suits to proceed, Goldman said. “Many of these lawsuits will now get dismissed,” he said. “The plaintiffs now are going to have to prove that the reasons for the rent concession did not exist at the time the rent concessions were offered.” The updated guidance is good news for tenants, REBNY Executive Vice President of Public Policy Basha Gerhards said in a statement. “Temporary rent relief can help New Yorkers stay in their homes and access new ones,” she said. “Clear rules help preserve the ability to offer temporary relief when tenants need it.” Eli Weiss, principal at Joy Construction , said the new DHCR guidelines will calm landlords’ nerves. “We only have one place to look for these regulations, which is the DHCR guidance,” he said. “Lack of guidance should not create industrywide lawsuits that have millions and millions of dollars in penalties behind them.” But landlords can’t count on the lawsuits disappearing altogether, Nathanson said: Rent concessions aren’t necessarily considered preferential rent, but there are still contexts where they might be, according to DHCR. And the new guidelines leave some ambiguity as to what those conditions are, he said. There is also an incentive for lawyers to keep pursuing some of the suits, he said. Cases against buildings that have rent-stabilized units but no 421-a subsidy can only try to recoup the amount that tenants allegedly overpaid, he said. But for buildings with the tax break, the suits claim they could pursue the amount that the developer hasn't had to pay in real estate taxes — meaning that a payout would be larger, Nathanson said. “I very highly doubt that the litigation that's currently open will stop,” he said. “I do wonder, though, if it slows down the seeming acceleration of new cases, because they have lost one of the big pillars on which their case stands.” Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register Related Topics: 421-a , Belkin Burden Goldman , Douglaston Development , Durst Organization , Eliot Spitzer , Fetner Properties , Gotham Organization , Joy Construction , REBNY , Rent Guidelines Board , Rent stabilized apartments , Rockrose , Spitzer Enterprises , Two Trees Management

items.title: Burger King Takes 'Have It Your Way' Approach To Restaurant Renovations
items.description: Burger King is asking customers to choose which restaurants it renovates first as the fast-food giant continues a multiyear effort to modernize its real estate portfolio. On Tuesday, Burger King announced the launch of ReBuildMyBK.com , a website that lets customers provide feedback on the physical condition and aesthetics of their local stores. The company’s goal is to use this feedback to decide which locations should be next in line for renovations to its modern “Sizzle” design. Pexels/Alicia Christin Gerald This is Burger King’s latest effort toward modernization since it began its push in 2022 under the company’s “Reclaim the Flame” turnaround strategy. This included a $250M investment in a modern image, new technology and kitchen equipment, according to a 2024 press release . The ultimate goal is to have 85% to 90% of U.S. Burger King restaurants modernized by 2028. The turnaround plan included Burger King's parent company, Restaurant Brands International, purchasing the chain's largest U.S. franchisee, Carrols Restaurant Group, for $1B in 2024. That deal brought more than 1,000 locations under the company-owned umbrella, but the company intends to sell them back to local operators after renovations are complete, CNBC reported earlier this month . When all is said and done, Burger King wants to have roughly 300 company-owned locations and another 6,000 owned by franchisees. As part of the initiative, Restaurant Brands International plans to invest up to $700M through 2028. Of that, it plans to use up to $550M for its Royal Reset program, which would include remodels, relocations, technology, building enhancements and kitchen equipment, according to Restaurant Brands International’s October earnings call . Executives also noted that stores with the Sizzle redesign generated an average annual unit volume of about $2.2M. Burger King’s ReBuild My BK campaign comes at a time when the chain outperformed other major fast-food competitors in the U.S. Its sales increased 8.4% during the third quarter, while McDonald’s saw a 0.2% decline and Wendy’s took a 5.7% drop . items.title: LAHSA To Return $150M Of HUD Funding In Finalized Settlement
items.description: A federal judge signed an agreement between the Department of Housing and Urban Development and the Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority , removing the LA program from HUD oversight. The settlement resolves an ongoing dispute in which HUD suspended payments to LAHSA amid a fraud investigation. The agreement requires LAHSA to give back about $150M in federal funding. HUD previously announced the deal, but it is now final, the agency said in a release Tuesday . The agreement also shifts federal money from LAHSA to the Los Angeles County government in stages, LAist reported , adding that the deal preserves the LA region’s request for $240M in annual federal funding for housing services. Pixabay/ValterM Databases and systems maintained by LAHSA will switch over to the county over the coming months, and tighter oversight will be implemented. “Today's settlement closes a difficult chapter for LAHSA and allows us to move forward with greater clarity and stability,” LAHSA interim CEO Gita O’Neill said in a release. “Our focus now is on working closely with our local partners to ensure continuity of services, support an orderly transition, and remain true to our mission of connecting our unhoused neighbors with the services, resources, and pathways to housing they need.” LAHSA has been the subject of scrutiny at the local level since at least 2024, when an LA County audit found that the organization mismanaged hundreds of millions of dollars for homeless services. Executives connected with organizations that received money from LAHSA were charged with misappropriating millions of dollars, including an instance of homeless funds allegedly being diverted to a nightclub . An LAist investigation last year showed that a former LAHSA co-CEO finalized a $2.1M contract with a nonprofit where her husband was an executive, despite telling the publication she was recused from the decision-making. HUD officials, including Secretary Scott Turner, pointed the finger for the removal directly at LAHSA. “Year after year, LAHSA funneled billions of dollars in federal funding to organizations with no oversight, which resulted in nothing but skyrocketing homelessness, failing at their most basic responsibility,” Turner said in HUD’s statement. But U.S. District Judge David Carter, who presided over the case, placed blame at the feet of both LAHSA and HUD. “This has been an absolute past dereliction of duty by the federal government,” Carter said at a Friday hearing, as reported by LAist. “I termed it a partnership in failure,” he said. “Local government turned an absolute blind eye to the distribution of these funds and transparency and accountability for these funds.” Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register
