items.title: Abandoned Property for Sale: How To Buy an Abandoned Home
items.description: Buying an abandoned property can be a bargain for homebuyers —if you can actually find such a property. Properties that are unclaimed by their owners are potential low-cost purchases that might be attractive to prospective homebuyers. They certainly have become all the rage on TikTok , with influencers snatching up properties left and right and sharing their renovation journeys. Still, "abandoned house for sale" isn't a sign you're likely to see on the roadside. (There might actually be laws against that!) An abandoned property is usually a property whose original owner is no longer in possession of the home. Due to the owner's financial difficulties, the house is typically run-down and in desperate need of repair. If the law in your area allows you to claim this type of home and you're handy, it might be worth investigating. However, some abandoned homes for sale can turn out to be in good condition, with the owner hoping to unload the property before foreclosure . This could provide the right buyer with an opportunity to purchase the abandoned property or unclaimed home at a discount—and possibly a significant return on investment if you later flip it. How to buy an abandoned property for sale near you Purchasing an abandoned or unclaimed property involves following the same procedures as buying any other piece of real estate. Before setting out on your journey to find an abandoned home, review your financial situation. Remember, there will be additional expenses over and above the original sale price of the property. A pre-qualification from your bank or lender will help you estimate what mortgage amount you qualify for. Many banks also require pre-approval letters , so you can make quick decisions on the property you wish to purchase. How to find an abandoned property for sale Most abandoned homes for sale are on their way to foreclosure, but the bank has not yet initiated the process. Various lists of abandoned properties or unclaimed properties are available, or you can search for abandoned foreclosures or pre-foreclosures online . Check for listings of homes for sale with certain phrases that might indicate an abandoned property, such as "immediate possession," "must sell," "below market value," or "under appraisal." Don't forget to add "near me." Real estate agents will usually have valuable knowledge of abandoned properties in the area and the law relating to claiming them, and can provide you with a selection of homes about to be foreclosed on by the bank. Some properties might look abandoned but are not listed for sale. You might also check into the laws regarding unclaimed property and whether there is a statute of limitations on its return. If you find an interesting unclaimed property like this, visit your county clerk’s office. It will have information about the homeowners, the home's current appraised value, liens, or tax problems. You could then try tracking down the owners and asking them to sell their property. If the property has had liens or tax problems, the owners might be more willing to sell. Risks involved with buying abandoned property Abandoned homes will almost always have issues. Due to months (or years) of neglect, a lack of maintenance, and overall aging, vacant homes are far from pristine. They are often sold as is, which means what you see is what you get. One major risk? Abandoned homes usually have had their utilities turned off. With no way to check the water, electricity, gas, heating and cooling systems, or appliances, even a professional home inspector will be unable to thoroughly evaluate the house. There could be wiring problems, water leaks, or gas leaks—any of which would be extremely costly to repair. It might be possible to have utilities turned on temporarily, but that requires paying a deposit and putting the utilities in your name. Even if utilities are turned on, you'll likely have to accept some elements of the abandoned home as is . But remember, forgoing major system inspections is a huge gamble. A second major risk factor is the deferred maintenance involved with the purchase of a property that's been left to the elements. If previous owners abandoned the home or lost it to foreclosure, they probably didn't pay attention to routine maintenance tasks . Costly repairs will crop up sooner than expected, and you'll have to budget for future repairs. And to top it off, obtaining home insurance on an abandoned home is difficult. Most insurance agencies won't insure a vacated house without an inspection from one of their agents. And that agent might require you to make costly repairs before issuing a policy. If the insurer issues a policy, premiums for an unoccupied structure will likely be significantly higher. Because no one has watched over the home, it's more likely to have suffered vandalism or fire damage. Vacant homes often have broken pipes or leaking roofs with resulting water damage, stolen copper wiring, mold, pest issues, and damaged appliances. Loading... The 14-story, 169-unit complex was acquired vacant and will be transformed into market-rate multifamily housing through a comprehensive renovation funded by the loan. Mark Reichter and Alec Frook of Gantry represented the borrower, a private real estate investor. An insurance company lender provided the three-year, fixed-rate loan. items.description: Zillow: CPI Shelter Forecast, November 2026 Zillow forecasts 3.0% rent inflation, 3.6% OER inflation annually in October, as measured by the Consumer Price Index. Written by Treh Manhertz on November 17, 2026 New shelter inflation numbers from the Bureau of Labor Statistics are scheduled to be released on Thursday, December 10, 2026 at 8:30 ET. Key Takeaway CPI housing inflation is expected to firm into the end of the year. We currently forecast annual rent inflation to finish 2026 around 3.0% and OER near 3.5%. Part of the year-end rise is mechanical, as the BLS folded October 2025's increase ,missed during the government shutdown, into April 2026. This adjustment will add about 0.3 points to the true underlying annual rate until April 2027. From last month's forecast, the year-end outlook was revised up for OER (3.44% to 3.53%) and down for rent (3.06% to 3.04%). New-lease rents have been growing at their fastest pace of 2025-2026, no longer pulling down housing inflation measures. items.title: A Better Credit Score Could Save Buyers $864 a Year on a Typical Mortgage
items.description: A Better Credit Score Could Save Buyers $864 a Year on a Typical Mortgage New Zillow analysis finds that in October 2026, buyers in the highest credit band got a mortgage rate 36 basis points lower than buyers in the lowest band Written by Kara Ng on November 17, 2026 Key findings In October 2026, buyers with a credit score of 740 or higher were quoted a 7.23% rate on average on a 30-year fixed mortgage. Those with a credit score between 680 and 739 typically were quoted a 7.45% rate, while those with a score below 680 on average were quoted a rate of 7.59%, a 36-basis-point spread between the highest and lowest credit bands. With a 20% down payment, the total monthly payment on a typical U.S. home in October, worth $364,812, would have been $2,656 in the lowest credit score band and $2,584 in the highest. That’s an annual savings of $864 for those with the best credit scores. As of October 2026, a median-income household with a score of 740 or higher could afford a $317,572 home, versus $308,924 for a score below 680. That gap puts about 21,500 more active listings within reach nationwide. A higher credit score can be worth real money. A buyer with a strong credit score (740 or higher) can save more than $800 per year compared to a buyer with a low credit score (300-679) when buying the typical U.S. home. Those savings would have brought about 21,500 additional listings within budget nationwide for a median-income household in October. A better credit score changes the affordability math Home buyers with higher credit scores often receive a lower mortgage rate on their loan, which means a lower monthly payment. In October, the average mortgage rate offered to buyers with strong credit scores was 7.23%, while buyers with low credit scores were quoted a 7.59% rate, on average. For a typical U.S. home ($364,812) with a 20% down payment, that would mean a difference of $72 in each month’s mortgage payment, or $864 a year. Buyers with good scores of 680 to 739 sat in between, with a 7.45% rate, on average. That means they would pay $348 a year less than someone with a low credit score, but $516 a year more than someone with a strong credit score. These savings stretch a home buyer's budget, bringing more homes within reach. In October, a median-income household with a low credit score could afford a $308,924 home — meaning it would spend no more than 30% of its income on housing costs — given the average mortgage rate on offer. If that same median-income household had a strong credit score, it could afford a $317,572 home, an increase of about $8,650 in buying power. Where a better score is worth the most A better credit score brings the biggest potential savings in coastal markets, where home values are higher. Across the 50 largest metro areas, moving from a low credit score to a strong one saves anywhere from $45 a month in Pittsburgh to $304 in San Jose. A home buyer in San Jose could save $3,648 a year by moving from a low credit score to a strong one, followed by San Francisco ($2,688), Los Angeles ($2,256), San Diego ($2,208) and New York ($1,740). San Jose buyers would also enjoy the largest gain in buying power from improving their credit score at $18,778, ahead of Seattle ($14,896), San Francisco ($14,602), Raleigh ($13,688) and Washington, D.C. ($13,489). The smallest annual savings are in Pittsburgh ($540), Oklahoma City ($576), Memphis ($576) and Cleveland ($588). These are markets where mortgage payments are relatively inexpensive already, so there is less room for improvement with a lower rate. October's rate gap was the narrowest of 2026 The 36-basis-point spread in mortgage rates offered to buyers with strong and low credit scores in October was the narrowest of the year. Across the first 10 months of 2026, the rate difference between the lowest and highest credit bands ranged from 36 basis points in October to 58 basis points in April, with a median of 46 basis points. The monthly payment gap ranged from $72 in October to $110 in April, with a median of about $88, so the typical buyer in the lowest band paid roughly $1,050 a year more than a buyer in the highest band over that stretch. Improving their credit score is not the only way a buyer can secure a better rate. Buyers can also compare offers from multiple lenders , yet few actually do. Among buyers who contacted a lender, 62% contacted only one, according to Zillow's 2026 Consumer Housing Trends Report . Methodology Rates come from Zillow's Custom Quotes marketplace and reflect 30-year fixed conventional conforming purchase loans with 20% down or more. Credit bands are 300-679, 680-739 and 740+, and rates are quoted nationally. Quotes do not come from Zillow Home Loans. Data is as of October 2026. Affordability is calculated for a median-income household in a given region. Monthly payment is the total estimated payment for a typical home in a given region with 20% down, including estimates for taxes, insurance and maintenance. items.description: Share: Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on LinkedIn I recommend visiting cushmanwakefield.com to read:%0A%0A {0} %0A%0A {1} Insights Bay Area Multifamily MarketBeat This MarketBeat report covers the SF Bay Area multifamily market for Q3 2026. Read the report for a detailed look at market conditions and trends. Download The Q3 2026 Report Key Takeaways Bay Area nonfarm employment increased YOY by 0.9% to over 4.0 million. Vacancy fell across the Bay Area for the 12th consecutive quarter, to 3.9%, as new construction has not been able to keep up with increasing demand. Net absorption has slowed in back-to-back quarters, as deliveries have been quiet, but remains positive, with 2,077 units absorbed in the third quarter. The pipeline, however, is growing, as units under construction have risen for five consecutive quarters, reaching 18,625 units through the third quarter. The effective rent as of the end of the third quarter was $2,982 per unit, up nearly 10% YOY. Economy: Solid Fundamentals Bay Area nonfarm employment increased year-over-year (YOY) by 0.9% to over 4.0 million. At the same time, the unemployment rate declined by 40 basis points (bps) to 4.1%. Employment growth is expected to continue rising over the next 12 months. Median household income increased by 6.7% YOY, to $153,800, remaining the highest of all metropolitan markets in the US. While tech layoffs have persisted, the artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) sector continues to expand its hiring and concurrently leasing large blocks of space. Through the third quarter of 2026, Bay Area-based companies captured 75.9% ($324.5 billion) of venture capital funding into AI/ML in the U.S. Supply and Demand: Demand Outpaces Supply Vacancy fell across the Bay Area for the 12th consecutive quarter, to 3.9%, as new construction has not been able to keep up with increasing demand. Vacancy is down 110 bps YOY and currently sits at the lowest level since the fourth quarter of 2007. Net absorption has slowed in back-to-back quarters, as deliveries have been quiet, but remains positive, with 2,077 units absorbed in the third quarter. As the number of available units continues to dwindle, absorption may continue to slow until new supply meets demand. Units delivered in the third quarter totaled 969, up 306 units from the prior quarter but down by over 500 units YOY. Excluding the prior quarter, it was the lowest quarterly total since the second quarter of 2013. The pipeline, however, is growing, as units under construction have risen for five consecutive quarters, reaching 18,625 units through the third quarter. There are over 100,000 units proposed across the Bay Area, but development is not likely to see a significant uptick in the short term as rising construction costs and a difficult financing environment prove to be headwinds. However, strong market conditions and state housing mandates may help to counteract these challenges. Pricing: Record Rents Rents have surpassed record highs yet again as vacancy continued to decrease. The effective rent as of the end of the third quarter was $2,982 per unit, up nearly 10% YOY. San Francisco County is responsible for much of this growth, as it reached $3,756 per unit in the third quarter, an increase of over 15% YOY. San Francisco is showing no signs of slowing down having posted YOY rental growth greater than 10% for three consecutive quarters, a feat that has not occurred since 2001. Economic Overview The Minneapolis–St. Paul economy showed signs of cooling in Q3 2026. Nonfarm employment held at just over 2.0 million workers, while the local unemployment rate climbed 30 basis points (bps) year-over-year (YOY) to 4.1%. At just 10 bps below the U.S. average of 4.2%, the gap between local and national labor market conditions narrowed, reflecting a departure from the metro’s longstanding pattern of outperforming national employment trends. Supply: Deliveries Slow as Pipeline Continues to Contract Deliveries totaled 1,070 units in Q3 2026, lifting year-to-date (YTD) completions to 3,267 units, nearly equal to the 3,364 units delivered in all of 2025, and pushing total inventory to 274,491 units. Units under construction shrank to 5,705 units, a 5.4% decline quarter-over-quarter (QOQ), as higher borrowing costs and uncertainty about the direction of debt markets kept new starts in check. Upcoming supply is largely confined to projects already underway. The starts that did proceed relied on financing already in-place or alternative capital sources, while conventional ground-up development remains difficult to launch. Demand: Homeownership Costs Support Rental Demand Renters absorbed 1,141 units in Q3 2026, below the 1,664 units recorded in Q2 2026 but roughly even with the 1,169 units in Q3 2025, lifting YTD absorption to 3,987 units. New inventory continued to lease without disrupting occupancy, with stabilized vacancy flat QOQ at 5.3% and 30 bps lower YOY. With conventional mortgage rates climbing back above 7.0% and home prices still elevated, ownership has moved further out of reach for households already priced out, keeping renters firmly anchored to rental housing and sustaining strong demand for the foreseeable future. Pricing: Rent Growth Slows as Owners Prioritize Retention Effective rents averaged $1,535 per unit and $1.80 per square foot (psf) in Q3 2026, representing 2.0% YOY growth as gains cooled across much of the market. Owners continued to work off concessions and prioritized occupancy and resident retention over aggressive rent increases. As a result, rent growth remained below operating expense growth and short of peak levels recorded two years ago, with performance strongest in select neighborhoods rather than broad-based across the metro. items.title: A conflict of interest
items.description: Non-QM loans are part of the equation helping investors expand their footprint in the property market. Financing edge: Five-year, interest-only loans can maximize rental margins over short hold periods. Market shift: As institutional investment retreats, mom-and-pop buyers stepped in, acquiring 20% more homes than they sold. Buyer fallout: Heavy investor demand keeps prices and rents high, contributing to locking gig and freelance workers out of ownership. Millions of Americans now embrace freelancing, small-business ownership, or gig-economy careers, but the industry hasn’t widely adopted lending structures that correspond to this shift. Add to that dynamic the increasingly unaffordable price tag for homes, and many would-be homeowners are stuck as renters. Many are renting from similarly minded entrepreneurs: mom-and-pop investors. The difference is that investors are turning to non-QM mortgages to finance property transactions, according to Cotatlity data. Many are doing so to take advantage of interest-only payments. The five-year flip The U.S. housing market offers an ideal proposition to small investors. Rents have increased 25% in the last five years, the federal government has curbed institutional investment, and home equity continues to rise. Investors are responding by reasserting their presence in markets across the U.S. Cotality data shows that the share of investors making home purchases has climbed since mid-2022 and now represents about a third of all transactions. Small investors represent about half of that transaction volume. Investment transactions occur frequently, making them an ideal candidate for interest-only loans. Nearly half of investor hold onto a property for five years or less — that precise timeframe makes an interest-only mortgage worth the equity tradeoff. Most interest-only loans have an initial period of five years before principal repayment begins where monthly commitments are reduced to create wider profit margins on rents. While investors who finance this way won’t reap the benefits of accrued equity, they can profit from the persistently high home prices and a tight inventory that makes short-term commitments profitable. How long does each investor type hold property Data source: Cotality, 2026 The U.S. is short 4.7 million homes . The ones that are available are in high demand. Add in mortgage rates near 7%, and affordability is being tested at its limits. Home prices reflect that squeeze. That dynamic has allowed investors in states like California, where they buy over a third of all homes, to profit on investments financed by interest-only loans. Investors nearly doubled the number of purchases they made in Los Angeles between Q1 and Q2 2026. Home prices jumped 2% during that period. This localized surge in investment is colliding directly with broader national price pressures—a dynamic we analyzed in our piece, Bend It Like Buyers. In major metros, that friction has created a stalemate between buyers and sellers, leaving the door open to more financially flexible investors. Many blame Wall Street. Institutional investors ban themselves Injecting corporate-backed demand into a market where local buyers are already stretched, extends even the most flexible buyers past their breaking point. Local residents who are priced out of home purchases find themselves competing with incoming industrial contractors for the exact same rental inventory. The resulting rent escalation drives up investor yields in the short term, but it simultaneously compresses local household purchasing power and accelerates affordability risk. That has a direct influence on local markets. In states like California, Texas, and Georgia, where investors buy over a third of all homes, prices have risen disproportionately. In Texas, home prices jumped 38% as investor share climbed to 31% between 2020 and 2023. In Georgia, prices jumped 54% alongside an investor share increase to 29%. But the passage of the 21 st Century ROAD to Housing Bill disrupted that playbook. Even before the passage of the bill, Cotality data shows that institutional investment contracted from around 250 home purchases a week to 100. Mom-and-pop investors filled the gap. Small-time landlords entered a market where equity was on the rise, which allowed them to build a cash cushion to insulate them from current high-interest rates and create wider profit margins that allow them to redeploy capital elsewhere. When that equity cushion is layered atop monthly rental income profit, these landlords can offset systemic hurdles such as interest rates and rising home insurance costs. Much of that extra capital is going into increasing their market share. Small mom-and-pop investors purchased 20% more homes than they offloaded last year, according to Cotality data. Their persistent presence is reshaping the housing market. Main street moves in Across the country, investors are the ones with the financial wherewithal to purchase homes in the current high-cost, high-rate environment. This is contributing to keeping costs — from home prices to rents — elevated and widening the gap for aspiring homeowners. Some renters will be blocked from homeowership by these costs. Others will bend and stretch to make the homeownership math work. Some will look to non-QM mortgages themselves. Forward-looking lenders who are optimizing for long-term growth will cater to both sides. There is now a path forward. It may be unconventional, but it is a door through which an increasing number of investors and homeowners are stepping to make the dream of homeownership a reality. items.title: Multifamily Rebalancing Advances
items.description: Multifamily Rebalancing Advances Nov 17, 2026 | 4 min read U.S. Multifamily Capital Markets | Q3 2026 Multifamily fundamentals continued to rebalance as occupancy edged higher, rent recovery broadened, and the construction pipeline contracted, creating a firmer foundation heading into 2027. Download the full report Experts David Amsterdam President, Capital Markets | U.S. David Goodhue Executive Managing Director | Boston & Head of Multifamily Capital Markets | U.S Rachael Rothman Director, National Capital Markets Research View All [5] Experts Share Article Top Highlights Occupancy continued to improve, edging higher to 95.7% despite more subdued leasing activity in the third quarter. Demand moderated from the exceptional second-quarter pace, with absorption trailing new deliveries but remaining well above year-ago levels. The development pipeline continued to contract, improving the longer-term supply outlook while near-term pressure remains concentrated in select markets. Rent recovery broadened across markets, with 40 of the Top 60 markets posting positive annual rent growth. Capital markets remain selective, as underlying transaction activity and pricing continue to reflect price discovery rather than a broad recovery in liquidity. Key Statistics Multifamily fundamentals remain resilient as the market continues to work through recent supply additions and the development pipeline moderates. Occupancy Remains Resilient National occupancy remained healthy in Q3 2026 as markets continued to absorb recently delivered units. While conditions vary across geographies, supply-constrained markets continue to demonstrate particularly strong operating fundamentals, while higher-supply markets remain more competitive. Source: Colliers Research, RealPage, MSCI Real Capital Analytics Rent Recovery Broadens Rent performance improved across a broader share of markets during the third quarter, signaling a more widespread recovery in pricing conditions. Performance remains uneven, however, with supply levels and local demand continuing to drive meaningful differences between markets. Supply Risk Remains Concentrated The national development pipeline continued to contract during the third quarter as financing challenges, elevated construction costs, and capital constraints limited new development. While the pullback should ease supply pressure nationally over time, several markets still face elevated construction pipelines that will continue to influence near-term performance. Capital Markets Navigate a Selective Recovery Investment activity continues to reflect a market in transition. Multifamily transaction volume reached $114.1 billion in Q3 2026, but the increase primarily reflected an entity-level merger rather than a broad recovery in liquidity. Excluding entity-level transactions, volume declined 7% to $44.5 billion, while apartment pricing remained under pressure. Investors continue to prioritize durable cash flow, realistic acquisition pricing, and manageable refinancing exposure as the market works through continued price discovery. Source: Colliers Research, MSCI Real Capital Analytics Sector Spotlight: Seniors Housing Seniors housing is benefiting from a combination of powerful demographic demand, improving operating performance, and constrained new supply. Growth in the older U.S. population is expanding the long-term demand base for independent living, assisted living, and nursing care, while limited development is supporting occupancy and rent fundamentals. Capital markets activity is also strengthening as investors respond to improving fundamentals and the sector's long-term demographic outlook. The report examines operating trends, regional performance, transaction activity, and the investment landscape across seniors housing and care. Looking Ahead Multifamily enters the final months of 2026 with healthy occupancy, a shrinking development pipeline, and a broader rent recovery, creating a more constructive operating backdrop. At the same time, capital markets remain selective, and refinancing pressure continues to create challenges and opportunities across the sector. Heading into 2027, the pace of new supply, local demand trends, and financing conditions will remain critical to determining where operating performance and investment opportunities strengthen most.
